prompt: Match each STRIDE threat to the property it violates.
A clinical note is edited and nobody can say who changed it. Which letter?

choices.text: T, because the note was changed
choices.why: The change was by somebody allowed to edit; what is missing is the record.

choices.text: R
choices.why: Right: repudiation, the missing record of who did what.

choices.text: I, because notes are confidential
choices.why: Nothing was disclosed.

choices.text: E, because staff have too much access
choices.why: Editing notes is within the role here.

prompt: Why is "SQL injection" not a STRIDE category?

choices.text: It is too rare to deserve one
choices.why: It is common; that is not the reason.

choices.text: It belongs under denial of service, as a kind of overload
choices.why: It can cause T, I or E as well.

choices.text: STRIDE predates SQL
choices.why: SQL is from the 1970s; STRIDE from 1999.

choices.text: A technique that causes several letters
choices.why: Right. STRIDE asks which property a part could lose, not which tool an attacker uses.

prompt: Three of STRIDE's properties are the CIA triad. What are the other three about?

choices.text: People: who they are, what they did, what they are allowed to do
choices.why: Right: authentication, non-repudiation, authorisation.

choices.text: Networks
choices.why: None of the three is about networks.

choices.text: Performance and cost
choices.why: Neither is a STRIDE property.

choices.text: The mechanisms: encryption, hashing and digital signing
choices.why: Those are mechanisms, not properties.

prompt: A phished receptionist password leads to every record being read. Where should the threat be filed?

choices.text: Under S only, because it starts with spoofing
choices.why: Any one letter will do; there is no rule that the first wins.

choices.text: Under all three letters, as three threats
choices.why: It is one threat with one chain; three copies triple the work.

choices.text: Under the letter that made you think of it
choices.why: Right. The letters overlap; they prompt, they do not file.

choices.text: Nowhere until the team agrees on the letter
choices.why: Debating the letter is time not spent finding the next threat.

prompt: Which kind of element is exposed to all six letters?

choices.text: A data store holding personal data
choices.why: Stores get T, I, D, and R when they are logs.

choices.text: A data flow crossing a boundary
choices.why: Flows get T, I and D.

choices.text: A process
choices.why: Right, because it runs code.

choices.text: An external entity
choices.why: Entities get S and R.

prompt: Which letters apply to a data flow in STRIDE per element? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: S
choices.why: Spoofing a flow means spoofing its source.

choices.text: T
choices.why: Data can be changed on the way.

choices.text: I
choices.why: Data can be read on the way.

choices.text: D
choices.why: A flow can be blocked.

choices.text: E
choices.why: A flow runs no code to elevate.

prompt: When does repudiation apply to a data store?

choices.text: When the store is a log
choices.why: Right: tampering with the record of who did what erases the evidence.

choices.text: When it holds personal data
choices.why: That raises I, not R.

choices.text: When several processes write to it
choices.why: That is a question about privilege.

choices.text: Always, for every store
choices.why: Only for logs.

prompt: Using STRIDE per element, how many questions does the portal's level 1 diagram raise?
Why can a data flow not be spoofed in STRIDE per element?

choices.text: Encrypted flows cannot be spoofed
choices.why: Encryption does not prove who sent something.

choices.text: Flows are inside the system
choices.why: Most of the portal's cross a boundary.

choices.text: Spoofing only applies to people
choices.why: The gateway is a system and can be spoofed.

choices.text: Spoofing a flow is spoofing its source, a question for the source
choices.why: Right. The question is asked once, where it belongs.

prompt: Which flows does STRIDE per interaction look at?

choices.text: Every flow in the diagram, one by one
choices.why: That is closer to per element.

choices.text: Those that cross a trust boundary
choices.why: Right, together with the elements at both ends.

choices.text: Only flows carrying personal data
choices.why: The criterion is the boundary.

choices.text: Flows between two external entities
choices.why: Those are not even drawn.

prompt: Put the questions of a crossing in the order the lesson asks them, from sender to receiver.
items: S: is the sender who it claims to be?
T, I: can the data be changed or read on the way?
D: can the receiver be flooded or the flow cut?
E: can the receiver be made to do too much?

prompt: On the payment webhook, why is tampering on the way not the real problem?

choices.text: Anybody sends the request and writes what they like
choices.why: Right: with S open, T on the way is moot.

choices.text: HTTPS already makes the whole webhook safe from start to finish
choices.why: HTTPS protects the way, not who sends.

choices.text: Tampering does not apply to flows
choices.why: It does: T is one of a flow's three letters.

choices.text: The gateway never sends webhooks
choices.why: It does; that is flow 7.

prompt: Six questions on flow 7 gave one serious threat, two to check and three answered. What does the lesson draw from that?

choices.text: Five of the six questions were wasted
choices.why: Answered questions are coverage, not waste.

choices.text: The serious one could not hide in an unasked category
choices.why: Right. The value is coverage, not a threat per question.

choices.text: Webhooks only need the S question
choices.why: Knowing that needs the other five asked.

choices.text: Per interaction finds fewer threats than per element
choices.why: The lesson draws no such comparison.

prompt: How many threats did the team write down for the portal?
Which threat came from the fact that the reminder worker uses the database owner's password?

choices.why: That is the console answering from the internet.
That is the webhook.
Right: elevation through the worker.
That is a note changed with no record.

prompt: Only one tampering threat survived the afternoon. What does carla's note conclude?

choices.text: That Vereda's integrity is in good shape
choices.why: That was the other possible reading, and she did not take it.

choices.text: That tampering is rare in web systems
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so.

choices.text: That STRIDE cannot find tampering
choices.why: It found one; the question is why only one.

choices.text: That tampering is the letter the team understands least
choices.why: Right, and lesson 5 comes back to it.

prompt: Which of these threats are about privacy rather than somebody breaking in? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: T08, the SMS that reveals treatment
choices.why: Nobody breaks in; the message discloses.

choices.text: T09, receptionists reading clinical notes
choices.why: Legitimate users seeing too much.

choices.text: T01, the forged webhook
choices.why: Somebody outside sends a forged request.

choices.text: T12, the console on the internet
choices.why: A stolen password used from outside.

prompt: Ten of the fourteen threats sit on flows. What do those flows have in common?

choices.text: They carry payment data
choices.why: Only one of them does.

choices.text: They cross a boundary
choices.why: Right: every one of them.

choices.text: They all reach the records database
choices.why: The webhook and the reminders do not.

choices.text: They all start at the patient
choices.why: Several start at the console or the worker.

prompt: Put the four parts of a threat statement in order.
Which of these is written as a threat?

choices.text: IDOR on the exams route
choices.why: A technique name on a route that may not exist yet.

choices.text: Exam security
choices.why: A topic; nobody can check it off.

choices.text: Attackers could read, change and delete exams
choices.why: Three threats in one sentence, and no who.

choices.text: A signed-in patient changes the exam number in the address and downloads another patient's PDF
choices.why: Right: who, what, to what, with what result.

prompt: Why does the lesson say to name the design rather than the bug?

choices.text: Before the code exists, only the design is real
choices.why: Right: a missing check is something a design can fix.

choices.text: Bugs are someone else's job
choices.why: The reason is about when the model is written.

choices.text: Bug names are too technical for daniel to follow in a meeting
choices.why: Readability is not the argument.

choices.text: Scanners already list every bug
choices.why: They do not, and that is not the reason.

prompt: When the team tried to write "the database" as a sentence, what happened?

choices.text: It became T13, the worker as owner
choices.why: That is one of the three, not all of it.

choices.text: It was dropped as a duplicate of T04, the exam files
choices.why: T04 is about the exam files.

choices.text: It became three threats with three fixes
choices.why: Right: T05, T09 and T13.

choices.text: It stayed a topic, kept for the risk numbers of lesson 9
choices.why: Topics do not get risk numbers.

prompt: "Attackers could spoof, tamper with and read the webhook." What is wrong with it?

choices.text: Webhooks cannot be read
choices.why: They can, on the way, if not encrypted.

choices.text: It names the design and not the bug
choices.why: That would be right, not wrong.

choices.text: It is three threats; the first fix would tick off all three
choices.why: Right. One threat per sentence.

choices.text: It should say T01
choices.why: The id is filed after the sentence is right.

prompt: How many findings did pytm 1.4.0 report for the portal?
Why do the portal and the staff console get the same 47 findings?

choices.text: The model describes them the same way
choices.why: Right: nothing in it says one reads every record.

choices.text: They run the same code
choices.why: They are separate applications.

choices.text: pytm gives every server 47 findings, whatever it is
choices.why: The count depends on the attributes declared.

choices.text: They share a database
choices.why: So does the worker, which got 34.

prompt: Why does PHP Remote File Inclusion appear on a console with no PHP?

choices.text: The console has a PHP component nobody noticed
choices.why: There is no PHP anywhere at Vereda.

choices.text: pytm assumes every server runs PHP by default
choices.why: It does not know what runs; that is the point.

choices.text: It was added to the model by mistake
choices.why: Findings come from the library, not the model.

choices.text: Nothing in the model says otherwise
choices.why: Right. A rule fires on what is not declared.

prompt: Which of the hand-written threats can no pytm rule find, because the model does not hold the fact? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: T12, the console on the internet
choices.why: The model puts it in the cloud, as designed.

choices.text: T13, the worker as the database owner
choices.why: pytm has no attribute for the account used.

choices.text: T08, the SMS that reveals treatment
choices.why: What a message says is beyond any rule.

choices.text: T01, the forged webhook
choices.why: Content Spoofing comes close to it.

prompt: How does the lesson say the 196 findings are best used?

choices.text: As the threat model, sorted by severity
choices.why: That buries T01 among 196.

choices.text: As reminders, read by somebody who knows the system
choices.why: Right: an hour with them adds two or three questions.

choices.text: Not at all
choices.why: They are useful as input.

choices.text: As the list to hand the pentester before the engagement
choices.why: The lesson does not suggest it.

prompt: Vereda adds a feature: physiotherapists record a short video of an exercise and the patient watches it in the portal. Using STRIDE per element, which new element raises E?

choices.text: The converter process
choices.why: Right: only processes are exposed to elevation.

choices.text: The video store
choices.why: A store gets T, I, D.

choices.text: The flow carrying the video
choices.why: A flow gets T, I, D.

choices.text: The physiotherapist
choices.why: An entity gets S and R.

prompt: For the same feature, which threat statement is complete?

choices.text: Video privacy
choices.why: A topic.

choices.text: A patient changes the video id in the address and watches another patient's exercise video
choices.why: Right: who, action, asset, result; I on the flow that delivers it.

choices.text: Insecure direct object reference
choices.why: A technique name.

choices.text: Videos could be leaked
choices.why: No who, no how.

prompt: In STRIDE, the property that elevation of privilege violates is ___.
